original_summary: 11 Nimmt is a shedding card game. Players play numbered cards onto growing discard piles, each card higher than the pile top and within 10 of it, counting round from the highest number back to 1. A player who cannot play must take a pile. Taking a big pile earns bulls, which allow multi-card plays. Leftover cards score penalty ox-heads, and the lowest total wins.

review.evidence: In the reviewed variation a player may take on purpose by playing a non-fitting card. The player facing a size-1 pile takes it for about 1.33 ox instead of inheriting the forced size-4 pile at about 4.3. That holds whatever the opponents hold. The reflex policy 'take every size-1 pile' draws against sensible play and beats random play. Because the pile cap of 4 equals the player count in 4-player games, seat order alone also picks who faces the full pile.

Under the reflex take, each player's penalty is roughly the ox in the predecessor's hand. Hand ox has SD about 1.5, so two players differ by about 2.1 points from the deal alone. Choices move totals by fractions of a point, so a better player does not reliably win.

Once the reflex is found, the only refinements left are the order of dumping and the boundaries where the round start rotates. Bulls need 3+ card piles, which never form, so the reward mechanic is never used. A strong player has little room to improve.
There is rich material to infer: near-perfect card counting, with only 2 (3 players) or 7 (4 players) cards unseen. But the dominant reflex makes that inference almost irrelevant to the decision.
Penalties, bulls and the winner follow by arithmetic from the cards played. No judge is needed.
It is turn-based and text-only, with one hidden hand per player, a fixed 9 or 8 rounds and no board. Its step count is within the limits.

problems: P1: Voluntary takes make 'take every size-1 pile' a near-dominant reflex. It cannot be beaten by sensible play and it beats random play.
P2: A single pile with a cap equal to the player count (4 players) or in a fixed cycle (3 players) lets seat order decide who faces the full pile.
P3: Bulls require 3+ card piles that never form under the reflex, so the 'Hot Pile' build-up and the bull reward are decorative.
P4: Under the intended good play each penalty is roughly the predecessor's hand ox, so the deal decides the winner (lottery trap).
P5: Card-counting information exists but there is no decision that uses it. There is no real choice of where to play or which top to leave.

changes.what: Forced fitting, as in the original 11 Nimmt. You may take a pile only if no card in your hand can be placed on any pile with room.
changes.why: This removes the cheap dodge. Whoever holds a fitter must place it, so takes come from running out of fitters or from full piles, as the original intends.

changes.what: Two piles instead of one, each capped at 5 cards. Placing a fitting card on a full pile counts as a take. Each turn's choice is a card plus a pile.
changes.why: Ten slots fit neither a 3-seat nor a 4-seat cycle, and forced takes from empty hands come irregularly. Who faces two full piles therefore depends on play, not seats. Choosing which pile to feed and which top to leave restores the original's 'play onto any pile' decision.

changes.what: Use the two piles to block opponents and to time the full piles.
changes.why: Players can steer tops away from what opponents are likely to hold, judged by counting cards. They can also time when piles fill so that someone else is the one forced. This gives card counting something to act on.

changes.what: Each bull is worth -2, earned for taking a pile of 3 or more cards. When forced, the player chooses which pile to take and which card restarts it.
changes.why: A 5-card pile averages about 6.7 ox, or about 4.7 net of the bull. A 3-card pile is about 4.0, or 2.0 net. A 1-card pile is about 1.3 with no bull. The forced player faces a real choice, and piles do build to 3-5 cards, so bulls happen.

changes.what: Penalty comes only from piles you take, and the pile you take is built by everyone.
changes.why: A penalty is no longer one predecessor's hand passed on. Who is forced, and when, depends on blocking, timing and the forced player's choice of pile, so play rather than the deal sets the gap.

changes.what: Drop the voluntary-take mechanic entirely. Every simple policy is now restricted to fitting plays: always the lowest fitter, always the highest fitter, always pile A, or random.
changes.why: The reflex no longer exists. Each remaining fixed policy ignores where the tops will land and who will face full piles, so it can be steered into the forced takes. This was checked case by case in expected_effect.

keeps: Numbered cards with circular fitting: higher than the top and at most 10 above, wrapping from N to 1.
You must play if you can, and take a pile only when you cannot.
Ox-head penalties, with 11-style 'double' cards worth 3 and multiples of 5 worth 2.
Bulls as the reward for taking a big pile.
Several piles to choose among, with pressure building as piles grow.

recommendation.reason: Forced fitting, two capped piles and stronger bulls remove the reflex take and the seat cycle. They turn hidden-hand card counting into a real decision about where to play and when piles fill, all within the platform's limits.

variation.name: 11 Nimmt: Two Hot Piles
variation.summary: There are two piles and you must play a card that fits if you can. Piles cap at 5 cards. Placing on a full pile, or holding no card that can be placed, forces you to take a pile. Big takes earn bulls worth -2. The lowest score wins.
variation.rules:
CARDS. The deck has N cards numbered 1 to N: N = 30 with 3 players, N = 40 with 4 players.

OX-HEADS. Cards 11, 22 and 33 carry 3 ox-heads. Every other multiple of 5 (5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40) carries 2. All other cards carry 1.

SETUP.
- Shuffle once.
- Deal each player a private hand of H cards: H = 9 with 3 players, H = 8 with 4 players.
- Turn the next two cards face up. They start Pile A and Pile B, each of size 1.
- The rest (1 card with 3 players, 6 with 4) are set aside unseen and take no part in the game.
- Everyone starts with penalty 0 and bulls 0.

INFORMATION. You see only your own hand. Everyone sees both piles (their cards, top card, size and ox total), every card played and every take, and all penalties and bulls.

FITTING. A card c fits a pile with top card t if d = (c - t) mod N is between 1 and 10 inclusive. Example with N = 30: on a top of 25, the cards 26 to 30 and 1 to 5 fit.

ROOM. A pile has room if it has fewer than 5 cards.

PLACEMENT. A placement is a card from your hand that fits a pile with room.

ROUNDS. The game lasts exactly H rounds. In round r the seats act one after another, starting with seat ((r - 1) mod number of players) + 1 and continuing in seat order, wrapping round. Each seat starts 3 times (3 players) or 2 times (4 players).

TURN. On your turn you choose exactly one card from your hand and one pile (A or B).
- If you hold at least one placement, you must choose a placement: the card goes on top of that pile. The pile's size rises by 1 and its ox total rises by the card's ox.
- If you hold no placement at all, you must TAKE. You choose any card and either pile, and then:
  1. Add that pile's ox total to your penalty.
  2. If the pile had 3 or more cards, gain 1 bull.
  3. Discard that pile's cards out of the game.
  4. Your chosen card becomes that pile's only card (size 1, ox equal to that card's).
- The other pile is unchanged.
- Every turn removes exactly one card from your hand, so all hands empty at the end of round H.

BULLS. Each bull is worth -2 at the end. Bulls are unlimited and never move between players.

END. After round H, each player's final score = penalty - 2 x bulls. Cards left in the two piles count against nobody.
variation.objective: The lowest final score (penalty minus twice bulls) wins. If two or more players tie for lowest, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect:
Takes now happen only when a player is forced, either because both piles are full or because no card in hand fits a pile with room. Each turn's choice is therefore which fitting card to play and which pile to feed. Players feed the pile they want to fill before an opponent's turn, and they leave tops that opponents (judged by counting the cards already played) are unlikely to be able to follow. They also keep a fitter in reserve for when piles are near full.

When forced, the choice is real. A big pile costs about 6.7 ox but returns a bull (about 4.7 net). A small pile costs about 1.3 with no bull. The card you restart with sets the next fitting window.

Policy check. The reflex take is now illegal. 'Always the lowest fitter', 'always the highest fitter' and 'always pile A' each ignore which pile fills on whose turn and which top is left, so a counting opponent can steer them into the 5-card takes. Each loses a substantial share of games to sensible play, and random play loses most games.

Seat order. Ten pile slots and irregular forced takes break the fixed seat cycle, so seat order no longer picks the victim. The rotating start balances first turns.

Luck. The deal still shapes how many fitters a player holds, but penalties come from piles everyone built and from takes whose timing play controls. The deal is no longer one predecessor's hand passed straight on.

Talk is left out. Interests do conflict, but with hidden hands and no binding deals a message could only be an unverifiable claim about one's cards. That adds words rather than reasoning, and it risks two players ganging up to force the third.

balanced.evidence: TOTALS. With 3 players (N=30) there are 22 one-ox cards, six 2-ox cards (5 to 30) and two 3-ox cards (11, 22), so 40 ox in all and a mean of 1.33 per card. With 4 players (N=40) the total is 29 + 16 + 9 = 54. A 4-card pile averages about 5.3 ox. COST OF EACH WAY TO TAKE: a size-1 pile costs the top card's ox, at least 1 (about 1.33) and no bull. A size-2 pile costs at least 2 (about 2.7). A size-3 pile costs at least 2 net of the bull (about 3). A size-4 pile is a forced take costing at least 3 net (about 4.3). Fitting costs 0 now. THE MAIN DECISION, 3 players, the player facing a size-1 pile (rounds 1 to 3: 1→2→3→1→2…). If they fit, the pile is size 2 for the next player, who fits safely because they will not face size 4. The third player faces size 3 and fits for free. So the player who faced size 1 now faces size 4 and pays about 4.3. If they take instead, they pay about 1.33. Taking saves about 3. This holds whatever the opponents' cards are, because nobody downstream wants to reset. Most of the time a non-fitting card is in hand (each card fits with probability 10/29), so the move is usually available. The round-start rotation only shifts this at the 2 boundaries per 9 turns. REFLEX POLICY: 'whenever the pile has 1 card, play your lowest-ox card that does not fit (take)'. (i) Against sensible play it matches best play, so it draws or wins on the deal. (ii) Against random play it wins, because the random player fits about a third of the time and inherits 4-piles. Under this policy every turn is a size-1 take. Bulls (needing 3+ cards) are never earned, so the labelled reward mechanic is decorative. The 'Hot Pile' build-up the game is named for never happens. In 4 players the cycle length equals the player count: A always faces size 1, B size 2, C size 3, D size 4. Seat order alone, cut only by the rotation boundaries, picks the victim, so the player who would face size 4 resets early in the same way. Seat effects are small: seat 1 absorbs the starting card, and with 3 players the last player's final card is never charged. The defect is the near-dominant reflex take, not the seats.
balanced.verdict_reason: A cheap reflex (take every size-1 pile) is never worse than fitting for the player facing it and beats random play; the game collapses into passing ox-heads.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete and use arithmetic only. Fitting is (c - t) mod N in 1..10. Placement happens if the card fits and the pile size is under 4; otherwise the player takes. Penalty, bulls and score = penalty - bulls are all numbers the game keeps. The game is finite at exactly H turns per player (9 or 8 rounds, at most 40). The turn sequence is fully defined: rounds start at seat ((r-1) mod n)+1, giving 3p order 123|231|312… This is irregular across round boundaries but unambiguous. Turns are sequential by design. Each round has one choice per seat (at most 4 choice steps) and 14 steps (at most 20). There are 12 attributes, 1 hidden element (hands) and 0 random draws per round (one shuffle at setup). The game needs no board, clock or judge. Lacking talk is acceptable: interests conflict (who takes), but cards played and takes are public, so players can reason from the record rather than guess. Talk would be unbinding chatter about who should eat the pile.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: When all players follow the good strategy (take every size-1 pile), each player's penalty is roughly the ox of the cards the player before them in the sequence plays. Over a 9-turn period the predecessor pattern is 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→3, 3→1, 1→3, 3→1, 1→2, 2→1. So each seat receives about one other hand's worth of ox, fixed by the deal. A 9-card hand's ox total has mean 12 and SD about sqrt(9 × 0.356 × 21/29) ≈ 1.5. The difference between two players is about 2.1 SD-points, while every player's choices change totals by only fractions of a point. These choices are the order of dumping, since all your cards are eventually passed on, and the occasional boundary exploit. A 3-ox card (11, 22, and 33 in 4p) in an opponent's hand is about one point of luck. So the winner under good play is mostly the deal: who sits behind the hand with fewer 2- and 3-ox cards. There is genuine material to infer: near-perfect card counting, with only 2 (3p) or 7 (4p) cards unseen. But it has little to act on once the reflex take dominates.

required_changes: Remove voluntary takes: a player may play a non-fitting card (and take) only if no card in hand fits, as in the original 11 Nimmt. With about 97% of 9-card hands holding a fitter, the player facing a size-1 pile can no longer pay 1 to dodge the 4-pile, and the timing of when to keep fitters becomes the strategic core.

Or, if voluntary takes stay, make them cost: add a flat +2 to every take of a pile under 3 cards. A size-1 take then costs about 3.3 against about 4.3 for the 4-pile. Re-check the decision table so that neither option is strictly better for the player facing a size-1 pile.

Make the pile cap differ from the player count and from a multiple of it (e.g. cap 5 with 4 players, cap 4 with 3 players is fine only after the change above). Otherwise seat order alone fixes who faces the full pile.

Make bulls reachable and worth chasing: award a bull for taking a pile of 3+ cards at -2 each, or raise the cap. Then building a pile deliberately is a real trade-off and the 'Hot Pile' theme exists in play.

After the changes, show a simulated or worked table: the reflex take policy and the always-lowest and always-highest policies against sensible and random play must each lose a meaningful share of games.

balanced.evidence: PAYOFF TABLE FOR A TAKE (net = pile ox - 2 x bull). The minimum ox is 1 per card. Size 1: ox 1 to 3, no bull, net +1 to +3. Size 2: ox 2 to 6, net +2 to +6. Size 3: ox at least 3, bull, net at least +1 (up to +7). Size 4: net at least +2. Size 5: net at least +3 (5 cards with ox 1 to 3 each: up to 15 - 2 = +13). Every take therefore costs at least +1, so the -2 bull never makes taking attractive. Its only effect is to soften the cost of big piles. The labelled ordering 'lower is better, takes hurt' is consistent with these numbers. TAKE FREQUENCY (3 players). There are 27 turns. The piles start at size 1 and each holds 4 more cards, so at most 8 placements fit before both piles are full. Each take resets one pile and frees 4 more placements, so there are roughly (27-8)/4, about 5, forced takes, plus takes caused by cards not fitting. Each top fits 10 of the 29 other values (about 34%). With 2 piles, a hand of k cards has no placement with probability of roughly (0.44)^k, so fit failures matter mostly late, when hands are small. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE. Placement is compulsory, so the only freedom is which fitting card and which pile, plus which pile and card on a forced take. (a) 'Always lowest fitting card, pile A if possible': it ignores pile size. It routinely places the 4th card, leaving the next player a pile that has room for one more card. It also routinely fills a pile to 5 when the other pile is nearly unfittable for its own remaining hand. A sensible player who counts room and keeps flexible cards for late rounds forces it into most of the ~5 takes. It loses or draws often, so it does not never-lose. (b) 'Always highest card' and 'always pile B' have the same flaw and are mirror images. (c) There is no 'always pass' option: a pass does not exist. (d) On a forced take, 'always take the smaller-ox pile' is sensible, not thoughtless, and it does not decide the game alone. Which hand gets stuck depends on the earlier play. Against random play, a player who tracks fits and room avoids takes markedly more often. No option is strictly better whatever the opponents do: the best card depends on the pile sizes left for the next seats and on which cards remain unseen. SEATS. Starts rotate 1,2,3 / 2,3,1 / 3,1,2, repeated three times. Each seat starts 3 times (3 players) or 2 times (4 players, 8 rounds), so the opening edges cancel. The last turn of the game goes to seat 2 (3 players) or seat 3 (4 players). That is a small one-turn asymmetry: with one card left, that player has no choice. It is not a decisive edge. All players can win, and ties for lowest are draws.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete. Fitting is defined arithmetically: d = (c - t) mod N in [1,10]. A collision with d = 0 is impossible because the cards are unique. Room is size < 5. A placement is both fit and room. If any placement exists it is compulsory; otherwise the player takes, choosing any card and either pile, with a precise 4-step take sequence, and the chosen card starts that pile even if it would not fit. The case 'one pile full, a card fits only the full pile' is covered: there is no placement, so the player takes and may pick either pile. The game is finite: exactly H rounds, one card per turn, hands empty at the end. Scoring is pure arithmetic: penalty - 2 x bulls, lowest wins, ties are draws, and cards left in piles count against nobody. Limits: 18 of 20 steps; 4 of 4 choice steps (one sequential choice per seat per round); attributes about 15 to 17 (4 hands, 4 penalties, 4 bulls, 2 pile lists, pile tops and ox totals), at most 20; hidden elements are the hands plus the set-aside cards, at most 3; 0 random draws per round, with the shuffle at setup only; 9 rounds, at most 40. The check 'holds any placement' is a legitimate complex rule check for the referee and can also be computed. Sequential choice with a rotating start is supported. No board, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed. No talk is the right decision here. The interaction is card placement, and promises cannot bind. Players are not left to guess blindly: every card played is public, so opponents' holdings can be inferred. Talk would only add words. This is not a repeated fixed-length cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: There is substantial inference. With 3 players, 29 of 30 cards are in play: you hold 9, see 2 on the piles, and know the other 19 are split between two opponents plus 1 set-aside card. As cards are played you can narrow down which fits each opponent still holds. You can then fill a pile to 5, or leave it at 4, exactly when the next seat is likely unable to fit the other pile. With 4 players, 6 cards are set aside, so the inference is weaker but still meaningful. There is planning across rounds: keep flexible cards (ones that fit both tops) for late rounds, when small hands make fit failures likely; manage pile sizes relative to seat order; choose the cheaper pile on forced takes and weigh bulls against size-3+ piles. Estimated chance share is about 35-45% (3 players) to 45-50% (4 players), from the deal (clumped cards near the pile tops) and the face-up starting cards. When all players play well, the outcome is decided by hand quality and by who is caught at full piles. Seat rotation and inference let good play overcome a mediocre deal, so the random draw alone does not decide equal-skill games. A careful planner is clearly favoured over random or first-option play.
